criterion_notes.c1: Examines community and household water supply and service access in Qwaqwa (Maluti-a-Phofung Municipality), including piped municipal water supply, per capita water supply availability, emergency municipal and private water tanker delivery, and communal/private boreholes.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain reading vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading diverge. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, this would be 'yes' because the study examines water governance, municipal financial mismanagement, corruption in emergency tanker procurement, apartheid homeland institutional legacies, and fragmented dual governance between traditional leaders (Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act, 2019) and municipal spatial planners. Under the binding 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type mechanism clarification, however, this is 'no': the study is a disaster-vulnerability (Pressure and Release) analysis of macro-historical legacies, general municipal mismanagement/corruption, technical capacity loss, emergency response delivery failures, electricity load shedding, and uncoordinated land-plot siting physically atop buried water pipes. It does not examine a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing household water service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden for service applications, documentation or tenure requirements conditioning utility connections, tariff or cost-recovery rules, accommodation/discretion, disconnection/enforcement rules, or utility ownership/regulatory structure directly governing household access).
criterion_notes.c3: Mixed-methods empirical forensic case study combining primary qualitative data from 31 semi-structured individual and group interviews conducted in March 2022 (analysed via conceptual and relational content analysis) with desk research and quantitative time-series analysis of ERA5 precipitation (SPI3, SPI6, SPI12), national load shedding, census population, dam water storage levels, and pipe leakage estimates.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports water supply availability, reliability, quantity, and inequality outcomes, including estimated per capita municipal water supply falling from 106 l/capita/day in 2001 to 15 l/capita/day in 2016 and 26 l/capita/day in 2020, service interruptions from pump power failures and pipe bursts, shortfalls in emergency tank delivery (1,500 delivered of 5,000 paid), and differential household reliance on paid private water delivery versus waiting at home for municipal tankers.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and units of analysis (Qwaqwa / Maluti-a-Phofung Municipality residents and municipal water system, plus 31 interviewed stakeholders), compound biophysical and socio-political exposures, water supply/access outcomes, and mixed-methods forensic case study design (PAR + CLD) are all clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English.

raw_response.exposure: Interaction of 2015–2020 meteorological drought anomalies (SPI3, SPI6, SPI12), national electricity load shedding, population growth, apartheid spatial and economic legacies, infrastructure decay and technical capacity loss, municipal financial mismanagement and corruption in emergency tanker procurement, and uncoordinated spatial plot allocation between traditional chiefs and municipal planners
raw_response.outcome: Community and per capita water supply availability and reliability during the 2015–2020 drought (estimated per capita water supply dropping from 106 l/capita/day in 2001 to 15 l/capita/day in 2016 and 26 l/capita/day in 2020), piped water disruptions, incomplete emergency tank deployment (1,500 of 5,000 paid tanks delivered), and unequal household reliance on paid private water delivery or boreholes
raw_response.population_and_sample: Residents and municipal water system of Qwaqwa (Maluti-a-Phofung Local Municipality, Free State Province, South Africa); 31 purposively and snowball-sampled stakeholders interviewed in March 2022 alongside municipal/ward-level census and hydro-climatic time series
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). While this empirical mixed-methods study examines water supply and household water access outcomes in Qwaqwa during the 2015–2020 drought (satisfying c1, c3, c4, c5, and c6) and discusses broad water governance challenges under the plain wording of c2, it fails Criterion 2 under the 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism clarification. The exposures analysed are compound meteorological drought, national electricity load shedding, apartheid socio-economic legacies, chronic infrastructure maintenance failure and technical capacity loss, procurement corruption in emergency water tankering, and uncoordinated land-plot siting atop water pipelines by traditional chiefs—rather than a legal, regulatory, or administrative rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, documentation or tenure requirements for utility connection, administrative burden, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement/disconnection rules, or utility regulatory structure governing access).
raw_response.study_design: Mixed-methods forensic disaster case study combining semi-structured interviews (n = 31), desk research, quantitative time-series analysis (SPI, load shedding, census population, dam levels, leakage scenarios), Pressure and Release (PAR) framework, and qualitative Causal Loop Diagram (CLD)
